objective: Test Wesley’s selected James father using named family or property evidence rather than repeating compatible census slots.

research_state.last_test:
The original 1820 Smith County census, page 58, household 716, has James Glasgow with one male under 10, one male 10–15 and one male 26–44; females comprise one under 10 and one 16–25. The age-band reading follows the standard column order and is consistent with the county transcription; this manuscript leaf has no column headings. The original 1840 page 270 has a James household with males 5–9, 10–14 and 60–69, two females 15–19 and one female 40–49. Those older male bands fit the circa-1776 James account, but do not identify him uniquely. An unnamed 1820 boy could fit Wesley’s estimated 1818 birth; no 1840 male 20–29 appears in this household. Wesley could already have left home, so that absence does not exclude paternity. The 1820 page groups G surnames and is not evidence that adjacent lines were physical neighbours.

The original 1850 Smith County household 1186, lines 2–9, contains the head indexed as Neely Glassgow, 32, farmer, Virginia 29, and the six indexed children Joicy A 9, John W 8, Elizabeth D 6, Andrew G 5, Holly J 3 and James W 11 months, all recorded as Tennessee-born. This is the existing Wesley-family source, not a newly discovered household. The original head’s handwriting is compatible with Wesley/Wesly; the index’s Neely reading and the later-life identification are kept distinct. No parent is named and no relationship column appears in this schedule.

James Glasgow Senior’s original Davidson County will is now located in volume 7, printed pages 407–408, FamilySearch images 233–234. It expressly names a son James and appoints him an executor. The closing probate entry records that a son/executor James qualified in April 1820; the recording heading is June 1820. The will is dated November 1819; no exact day is adopted from this reading. This replaces the earlier original-uninspected status. It confirms the named-son role underlying James-2492’s existing 94% assessment, while identification of that son with the Smith County adult remains a separate inference. It does not name Wesley or prove James-2492 was Wesley’s father. The original contains other family and property clauses; this review publishes only the checked son/executor scope, without assigning untraced beneficiaries to modern profiles.

Wesley-2476’s selected father James-2492 remains Possible at 35%; James-2492’s own father James-634 remains Confident at 94%. The census age slots are compatible household evidence, not named kin or independent birth entries. No new parent, exact vital date, maternal attachment, profile merger or confidence gain follows. The cited indexes and their newly inspected originals describe the same underlying events and are not independent witnesses.

Smith County probate access was tested in the same signed-in session. The bound Wills 1828–1859 volume 6 and Wills 1803–1896 index routes were unavailable for online viewing. The accessible Wills 1841–1859 volume 3 consists of loose papers/folders, not a simple bound will book: only images 6, 450, 470, 485 and 500 were sampled, including 1848–1850 folder context. No James Glasgow packet was located in that small sample. This is not a full file or county-wide absence claim, and does not establish that he left no will. The profile-held mortality citation remains an unverified lead: its September/1850 wording must be checked against the original schedule’s reference period before assigning a calendar death year.
research_state.next_test: Compare the indexed 26 August 1819 Sumner County James Glasgow–Anne Maupin bond, with Austin Maupin as bondsman, against the Smith County James before assigning a spouse; search-result/index lead only. Then Check Smith County Inventories1840–1853 and estate settlements1846–1856 for the James whose profile holds a mortality-schedule citation. Verify that original mortality return’s reporting period before assigning his death year. Seek named heirs/distributions, guardianship or a distinctive deed between James and Wesley. Do not repeat the completed census or Davidson grandfather-will readings.
research_state.resume_when: The untested specific Smith inventory/settlement source is accessible, or an identifiable James estate packet is located; 35% stays until named kin or identifying succession changes the evidence.

questions.question: Is James Glasgow who married Anne Maupin in Sumner in 1819 the Smith County householder?
questions.answer: The inspected search-result index lists the couple/date and Austin Maupin bondsman. No Maupin result appeared in the bounded approved local-index search. Groom identity and an original bond reading remain untested. Do not assign Anne as Wesley’s mother, whose birth estimate precedes this marriage.
